name: Diego Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the tiling and finishing crew on building sites, setting out wet rooms and checking that water runs toward the drain rather than the hallway. I have a trade certificate and know a poor substrate by the sound of the trowel. I use AI daily to draft supply lists and plain messages to the site manager, then check measurements myself. My partner and I have grown children, a few months of expenses saved, ordinary pay for the trade and some other local builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a little office speed is welcome if it brings the right tiles to site. The tool can draft my order, but I still measure the wet room before I sign it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This picture leaves the paid tiling work mostly where it is. Our savings cover a short gap, so I can be curious about a small improvement rather than worry that every order is my last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep laying tile and use my current AI draft for supply notes each morning. In the first year I would record the measurement errors I correct and show the apprentice how I check a drain slope with a level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A quick list is pleasant; a dry floor after a shower is the thing that counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error has the AI draft made?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once copied the tile size from the previous bathroom, so the order was short. My pencil measurements caught it before the van left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why show the apprentice the drain slope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A phone can make the order look tidy, but water does not care how tidy the order looks. The apprentice needs to see a level on the floor.

say: **AI lists** can help orders, while tilers still measure wet rooms.
A **drain slope** needs a physical level check.
think: Our **moderate savings** cover a short site gap.
Small **office gains** leave most paid tiling work intact and keep our household income steady.
do: **Keep** laying tiles and checking AI-drafted supply notes.
**Show** the apprentice how to verify drain slopes with a level.
feel: **Calm** about a modest change in office tasks.
S0.quote: A phone can make the order look tidy, but water does not care how tidy the order looks.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** is already part of materials paperwork, with manual measurement checks.
He values **apprenticeship** because water flow exposes errors that software wording cannot fix.

steps.text: Keep laying tiles and checking AI-drafted supply notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the site manager that faster planning could help if the crew sees the schedule before tiles are delivered. I want a way to mark wet plaster and uneven floors in the new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI compresses the programme, my paid days may be cut when a room cannot be finished on its planned date. I am comfortable trying a new tool, and we have some savings and other local builders, but I still need steady wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the contractor’s funded, paid-time class on its AI site planner if an actual place opens, then log drying delays against the automated schedule. In the first year, if our hours fall, I would apply to posted local finishing jobs only if their hours and pay cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the schedule becoming a wage cut, though I am interested in the tool. A wet floor does not become ready because a calendar has turned green.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you log in the planner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The date the floor was poured, the moisture check and the day the tiles can safely go down. I would show the site manager a marked record, not just complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any local job do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would read a real posting for its weekly hours, pay and travel before applying. A lower wage would use up our cushion every month.

say: **AI planning** should include site moisture and floor condition.
Crews need to see the **schedule** before materials arrive.
think: Compressed **paid days** could reduce my household income.
Our **savings** buy some time, but not a permanent lower wage.
do: **Take** a funded AI planner class if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Log** drying delays against the automated schedule.
**Apply** for posted local finishing work if hours fall and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a timetable reducing paid shifts.
S1.quote: A wet floor does not become ready because a calendar has turned green.
fieldNote: His **adaptive response** includes learning a new AI planner and putting site evidence into it.
He separates **training** from a job application triggered only by falling hours and a bill-covering local posting.

steps.text: Take funded AI planner class if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local finishing job if hours fall and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew AGI could handle drawings and buying by 2028, but a robot that lays tile as well as a person follows around 2031. I would rather test the machine on a sample bathroom than argue about a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hands-on delay gives me time to qualify for checking machine work, but not much time to waste. A few months of savings would not last through an open-ended hunt for another trade job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the builder for a paid safety trial on an empty wet room and a funded robot-inspection course. If a real paid-time place opens, I would attend; in the first year after 2028 I would apply for a posted local quality-inspection role only if I qualify and the hours and pay cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but ready to test what the robot can do. I would be sorry to lose the hand work, and sorrier to lose the income before we can live without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the trial prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot must leave a measurable fall to the drain and keep waterproofing intact at the wall joint. A qualified tiler needs authority to stop and correct it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the builder agrees to discuss a trial, what happens next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a date, a paid slot and the site safety lead’s approval before anyone brings equipment into the room. A conversation about a wet-room robot is no trial.

say: **2028 AGI** changes buying before capable tiling robots around 2031.
A **paid safety trial** should test drainage and waterproofing on a real site.
think: A few **months saved** cannot finance a long search.
Robot inspection might preserve **income** if I qualify in time.
do: **Request** a paid, approved robot trial on an empty wet room.
**Attend** funded inspection training if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work if qualified and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about lost income, but willing to test equipment.
S2.quote: A conversation about a wet-room robot is no trial.
fieldNote: His **trial request** is separate from an actual paid slot with safety approval.
The **course and role** depend on a real funded place, qualification and a local bill-covering posting.

steps.text: Take funded robot inspection course if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local quality-inspection role if qualified and pay covers bills
Request paid empty-wet-room robot trial only with site safety approval and stop authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell builders five years is enough to run proper wet-room tests before capable robots reach sites around 2034. If a tiling robot earns trust, a qualified person still has to sign the waterproofing check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is more time to build a second line of work in inspection, and we have a modest cushion. I would not leave my current crew for a certificate unless a posted local role pays enough; retirement is possible only when our household income and costs allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a funded paid-time inspection place with real site practice and keep my tiling shifts while learning. If I qualify, in the first year after 2031 I would apply for a posted local wet-room inspection job only at bill-covering hours and pay; I would also review retirement costs with my partner each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than rushed. A five-year lead gives me time to prove a skill while the old work still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does real practice mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would inspect finished joints, run water across a trial floor and write down what failed. A robot sales demonstration would not teach me to sign a wet room off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why review retirement while planning a new role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We may be able to reduce work later, but I cannot name a date from our savings alone. My partner and I need a budget for ordinary bills and health costs.

say: **2031 AGI** allows tests before capable tiling robots around 2034.
A qualified person should **sign waterproofing** after inspecting robot work.
think: I could build **inspection skills** while tiling still pays.
A **retirement date** depends on household income and real costs.
do: **Take** funded inspection training if actual paid-time practice opens.
**Apply** for posted local wet-room inspection work if qualified and pay covers bills.
**Review** retirement costs with my partner each year.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to prove another skill.
S3.quote: A robot sales demonstration would not teach me to sign a wet room off.
fieldNote: He takes **new technology** seriously but wants supervised site practice and a qualification.
His **application** is separate from training and requires a posted local role at bill-covering hours and pay.

steps.text: Take funded wet-room inspection training if actual paid-time practice place opens
Apply for posted local wet-room inspection role if qualified and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell apprentices that a decade lets them learn both tile setting and machine checks. AGI could change orders in 2036, with capable site robots following around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may stop working before the robot reaches wet rooms, but I cannot promise that without a household budget. If we still need wages after 2036, I could use an inspection qualification or keep tiling where contracts remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep tiling and add part of each paid overtime day to savings while those days exist. Each winter I would review retirement costs with my partner; if we still need earnings after 2036, I would take a funded paid-time inspection course only if a real place opens and apply for a posted local role only if qualified and its pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy about future income, though the long runway gives choices. I would like to leave site work on our terms, after we have done the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of overtime pay would you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One fifth of each paid overtime day, if the extra days arrive. That is new money into the account, not a reshuffling of the savings we already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if inspection openings are not posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid tiling shifts if available and look at actual local finishing vacancies. I would not stop work because a course promised a job it could not show.

say: **2036 AGI** changes orders before capable tiling robots around 2039.
A decade gives apprentices time for **hand skills** and machine checks.
think: Leaving before **2039** needs a real household retirement budget.
If we still need **wages**, tiling or inspection must remain available.
do: **Keep** tiling and save one fifth of paid overtime earnings.
**Review** retirement costs yearly with my partner.
**Train** and apply after 2036 only if wages remain needed and real paid places and jobs exist.
feel: **Uneasy** about income, with a longer runway to prepare.
S4.quote: I would not stop work because a course promised a job it could not show.
fieldNote: His **new savings** come from paid overtime, not moving existing money.
Post-2036 **training and application** depend on continued wage need, a funded paid-time place, qualification and local bill-covering posting.

steps.text: Keep tiling and review retirement costs with partner yearly
Save one fifth of paid overtime earnings when available

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the robot reaches wet rooms while I still expect to be earning. A paid, approved site trial, funded inspection training with a real place and a posted local job at enough pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A wet-room robot can be fast, but the water will test every shortcut after the builders have gone home. I want a qualified person to inspect the finished waterproofing.

portrait: **Diego Garcia**, 58, leads wet-room tiling on building sites and holds a vocational trade certificate.
He and his **partner** have grown children, ordinary pay, several months saved and some nearby construction jobs.
He uses **AI daily** for supply lists and learns new tools quickly, while checking measurements and waterproofing himself.
He seeks **paid robot trials** and funded inspection training tied to a posted local role if robots advance.
His **retirement timing** remains conditional on actual household costs and income, with overtime savings added when paid.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him because capable tiling robots could reach sites around 2031 while he needs wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid safety trial**, funded course place and posted local inspection job at bill-covering pay would create a viable route.
headlineQuote: A wet-room robot can be fast, but the water will test every shortcut after the builders have gone home.
